subject: history
topicDisplay: The development of Church, state and society in Medieval Britain 1066-1509

questions.lo: The Norman Conquest of 1066
questions.q: In which year did the Norman Conquest take place, when William of Normandy invaded England?
questions.explain: 1066 is one of the most famous dates in English history. Edward the Confessor died with no son, and William of Normandy invaded and won the throne.

questions.lo: The Norman Conquest of 1066
questions.q: At which battle did William of Normandy defeat King Harold Godwinson?
questions.explain: The Battle of Hastings (October 1066) ended with Harold's death and William's victory. William was crowned on Christmas Day 1066 and became William the Conqueror.

questions.lo: Controlling England: castles and the Domesday Book
questions.q: What was the Domesday Book of 1086?
options: A book of prayers used by monks
A survey recording who owned land, so the king could tax people
A list of everyone who died in the Black Death
The rules of the feudal system written by the Pope
questions.explain: The Domesday Book was a giant survey of who owned what land and what it was worth, so William could tax fairly and know the value of his kingdom.

questions.lo: Controlling England: castles and the Domesday Book
questions.q: Why did the Normans build motte-and-bailey castles so quickly after 1066?
options: To store the Domesday Book safely
To let a small number of soldiers control a large, unhappy population
To house the Pope when he visited England
questions.explain: The Normans were a small ruling group. Quick earth-and-wood castles let a few soldiers dominate an area and keep control of a much larger population.

questions.lo: Society and the feudal system
questions.q: In the feudal system, which group was at the very bottom of the pyramid?
questions.explain: The pyramid ran king to barons to knights to peasants. Peasants were the vast majority; they worked the land and were not free to leave.

questions.lo: Society and the feudal system
questions.q: A baron is granted land by the king. In return, what was a baron expected to provide?
options: Loyalty and knights to fight for the king
questions.explain: Feudalism worked as an exchange: the king granted land to barons, who in return gave him loyalty and provided knights for his army.

questions.lo: Christendom and the power of the Church
questions.q: Who was the head of the Church across medieval Christendom?
questions.explain: Almost everyone in Western Europe was Christian and followed the Pope in Rome, the head of the Church. This shared faith was called Christendom.

questions.lo: Christendom and the power of the Church
questions.q: The murder of Archbishop Thomas Becket in 1170 is a famous example of which kind of struggle?
options: A war between England and France
A clash between the Church and the Crown over power
A fight between two royal families for the throne
questions.explain: Becket, the Archbishop of Canterbury, clashed with King Henry II. His murder is the classic example of the medieval struggle between Church and Crown over who held more power.

questions.lo: The power of the monarchy: King John and Magna Carta 1215
questions.q: In which year did King John's barons force him to seal Magna Carta?
questions.explain: Magna Carta ('the Great Charter') was sealed in 1215 after King John lost wars, raised heavy taxes and angered his barons.

questions.lo: The power of the monarchy: King John and Magna Carta 1215
questions.q: Which statement about Magna Carta is the MOST accurate?
options: It gave every peasant the right to vote
It established the important idea that even the king must obey the law
It made the Pope the ruler of England
It ended the feudal system overnight
questions.explain: A common mistake is thinking Magna Carta gave rights to everyone. It mostly protected barons and free men. Its lasting importance is the principle that the king is not above the law.

questions.lo: The origins of Parliament
questions.q: Which baron called the 1265 Parliament that helped shape the Parliament we know today?
questions.explain: In 1265 Simon de Montfort called a Parliament that, for the first time, invited townspeople and knights of the shires, not only lords and bishops.

questions.lo: The origins of Parliament
questions.q: Why is Simon de Montfort's Parliament of 1265 seen as an important step?
options: It removed the king from power completely
It invited ordinary townspeople and knights, not just great lords
It abolished all taxes in England
It gave women the right to vote
questions.explain: For the first time ordinary townspeople and knights of the shires were invited, spreading a share of power beyond the lords and bishops.

questions.lo: The Black Death 1348 and its impact
questions.q: The Black Death reached England in 1348. Roughly what fraction of the population did it kill?
options: About a third to a half
questions.explain: The plague killed around a third to a half of England's population within a couple of years. People did not understand germs and often blamed 'bad air' or God's anger.

questions.lo: The Black Death 1348 and its impact
questions.q: What surprising effect did the Black Death have on the peasants who survived?
options: They lost all their power to the lords
Because workers were now scarce, they could demand higher wages
They were all forced to become knights
It had no effect on ordinary people at all
questions.explain: With so many dead, surviving workers were in short supply. This raised peasants' bargaining power, and lords had to offer better pay to keep them.

questions.lo: The Peasants' Revolt 1381
questions.q: Who led the Peasants' Revolt of 1381?
questions.explain: Wat Tyler led thousands of peasants who marched on London in 1381. He was killed when the rebels met the young King Richard II.

questions.lo: The Peasants' Revolt 1381
questions.q: Which grievance helped cause the Peasants' Revolt of 1381?
options: A hated poll tax and attempts to freeze wages
questions.explain: A new poll tax charged every person the same amount, hitting the poor hardest, and lords tried to hold down wages after the Black Death. Both fuelled the revolt.

questions.lo: The Wars of the Roses and the end of the medieval period
questions.q: The Wars of the Roses were fought between which two branches of the royal family?
questions.explain: The House of Lancaster (red rose) and the House of York (white rose) fought civil wars for the throne in the late 1400s.

questions.lo: The Wars of the Roses and the end of the medieval period
questions.q: At the Battle of Bosworth in 1485, Henry Tudor defeated Richard III and became which king?
options: Henry VII, the first Tudor king
questions.explain: Henry Tudor won at Bosworth in 1485 and became Henry VII, the first Tudor king. Historians often use 1485 to mark the end of medieval England.

questions.lo: How historians use evidence
questions.q: The Bayeux Tapestry shows the events of 1066 and was made close to that time. What type of source is it?
options: A secondary source written in the 1900s
A source about the Peasants' Revolt
questions.explain: A primary source is made at or close to the time of the events. The Bayeux Tapestry is primary; a modern textbook written later would be a secondary source.

questions.lo: How historians use evidence
questions.q: A monk writes a chronicle describing rebels as wicked and evil. What should a historian ask about this source?
options: Nothing, because monks always told the truth
Who wrote it, when, and why it might be biased
Only whether the handwriting is neat
questions.explain: Historians weigh up sources by asking who made them, when, and why. A monk might be biased against rebels, so his words are not automatically the whole truth.
